item.title: A pilot randomized controlled trial assessing the feasibility and preliminary effects of a text message intervention to promote secure storage and disposal of prescription opioids
item.description:
Background: Unused prescription opioids are a major source of diversion and nonmedical use, yet adoption of secure storage and disposal practices remains low. Scalable behavioral interventions are needed to promote medication safety. We pilot tested a theory-informed short message service (SMS) text-based intervention designed to encourage secure storage during treatment and disposal of unused prescription opioids following treatment.

Methods: We conducted a two-arm, single-blinded randomized controlled pilot trial (June-December 2024) among adults prescribed an opioid medication (≤30 days). Participants (N = 479) were randomized to receive a 45-day SMS intervention or standard care. Surveys were administered at baseline, mid-intervention, and post-intervention. Primary outcomes were self-reported locked storage (mid- and post-intervention) and disposal of unused medication (post-intervention). Feasibility metrics included recruitment, retention, intervention delivery, and acceptability. Logistic regression models assessed group differences using a modified intention-to-treat approach.

Results: Recruitment via electronic health record outreach was feasible, and retention was reasonable (76.6%). Most intervention participants reported the messages were helpful, acceptable, and non-burdensome. A higher proportion of intervention participants compared to control reported storing opioid medications in a locked location. The pilot study was underpowered to detect differences between conditions for disposing of unused medication.

Conclusion: A theory-informed SMS intervention to promote opioid medication safety was feasible, acceptable, and associated with improved storage behaviors. Findings support further evaluation through a hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial.

Egan KL, Cox MJ, Helme DW, Jackson JT, Paukner LD, Kline DM

item.title: Independent and interactive association of reported impairment in fatal crashes among young California drivers: A cross-sectional analysis
item.description:
Objective: To examine the independent and combined associations of reported alcohol, drug, and fatigue involvement with crash fatality among young drivers in California.

Methods: Using 2016-2024 injury crash data from the University of California, Berkeley Transportation Injury Mapping System, we performed logistic regression to examine the association between reported driver impairment and crash fatality among drivers aged 15-24. Additive interaction was assessed using binary impairment indicators and interaction terms. Relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated from adjusted odds ratios (AORs) using the delta method.

Results: Among 308,512 injury crashes, including 3907 (1.3%) fatalities, most drivers had no reported impairment (84.8%), followed by reported alcohol-impaired (11.4%), and males comprised the majority across all impairment categories. Fatality odds were significantly increased for reported drug-impairment (adjusted OR [AOR] = 20.35, 95%CI: 18.18-22.77, p < .001) and alcohol-impairment (AOR = 4.65, 95%CI: 4.28-5.06, p < .001), with fatigue approaching significance (AOR = 1.27, 95%CI: 0.98-1.63, p = .07). Jointly reported alcohol and drug impairment significantly increased fatality odds (AOR = 65.72, 95%CI: 57.24-75.45, p < .001) and had strong evidence of synergistic interaction (RERI = 41.80, 95%CI: 32.95-50.65). No significant interaction was observed between reported alcohol and fatigue.

Conclusions: Reported substance-related impairment significantly increased fatal crash risk among California young drivers, with alcohol-drug co-use associated with synergistically elevated risks. Preventing polysubstance use presents an urgent opportunity for youth-focused interventions targeting risky driving behaviors among young drivers.

Lotito A, Vaca FE, Li MS, Hu S, Hill L, Griswold J

item.title: Combination bupropion-zonisamide facilitates rapid reduction in smoke exposure and prevents weight gain during switching to electronic nicotine delivery systems: A randomized clinical trial
item.description:
Introduction: A pilot study suggested that the combination of bupropion (BUP) and zonisamide (ZON) could facilitate smoking reduction during switching to an electronic nicotine delivery system (ENDS). This randomized controlled trial tested the hypothesis that BUP/ZON would produce greater smoking reduction than BUP alone or placebo (PLAC).

Methods: Adults who smoked cigarettes, but were not seeking cessation treatment, were asked to switch to ENDS provided during study Weeks 1-12. Participants were randomized to receive BUP/ZON, BUP, or PLAC (N = 60 per group) during Weeks 2-8. Assessments included exhaled carbon monoxide (eCO), self-reported cigarette and ENDS use, dependence level, withdrawal symptoms, reward ratings, body weight, and adverse events. Outcomes were analyzed using modified intent-to-treat (mITT), complete-case, and per-protocol treatment-adherent samples (≥80% medication adherence).

Results: The mITT analysis showed no treatment differences in end-of-treatment eCO but higher smoking abstinence rates in both active treatment groups than PLAC (26.7% BUP/ZON, 25.0% BUP, 10.0% PLAC). In the per-protocol sample, eCO was significantly lower with BUP/ZON than with BUP or PLAC. Early reductions in eCO during the first treatment week-more common with BUP/ZON-strongly predicted later outcomes. Exploratory complete-case analyses showed lower tobacco dependence and craving in BUP/ZON than control groups. Weight gain occurred in BUP and PLAC, whereas weight loss was observed in BUP/ZON.

Conclusions: Bupropion plus zonisamide shows promise for smoking reduction and cessation, particularly when medication adherence is maintained. Prevention of post-cessation weight gain may offer additional clinical and public health benefits. Larger trials with longer treatment duration are warranted.

Rose JE, Behm FM, Willette PN, Botts TL, Botts DR

item.title: Nicotine vaping and conventional tobacco product use among adults in the United States stratified by substance use disorder severity: A cross-sectional analysis
item.description:
Background and aims: Although nicotine vaping is common in the general population, prevalence of vaped nicotine among people with varying severity of alcohol use disorder (AUD) or drug use disorder (DUD) has not been well-characterized. We aimed to characterize the use of vaped nicotine and conventional tobacco products amongst US adults with substance use disorder (SUD) stratified by SUD severity.

Methods: This was a cross-sectional study using nationally representative survey data from 92,233 adults in the United States from the pooled 2022 and 2023 National Surveys on Drug Use and Health. We compared rates of nicotine vaping and conventional tobacco product use (i.e., cigarettes, cigars, pipes, and smokeless tobacco) alone and in combination among adults with AUD and/or DUD and stratified results by SUD severity.

Results: Use of vaped nicotine alone (10.8%) and in combination with conventional tobacco products (13.0%) was common among individuals with SUD. After adjusting for age, increasing severity of DUD was associated with greater odds of any tobacco product use. Additionally, each one-level increase in DUD severity (none, mild, moderate, severe) was associated with higher odds of vaping nicotine with (aOR 3.3, 95% CI 3.1, 3.5) or without (aOR 2.4, 95% CI 2.2, 2.5) co-use of conventional tobacco products, compared to no tobacco use. Similar trends were observed among those with AUD.

Conclusions: Overall tobacco product use including vaping increased with severity of SUD. Strategies to integrate tobacco cessation with SUD treatment should consider vaped and conventional tobacco products and tailoring cessation treatment for SUD severity.

Bredenberg E, Binswanger IA, Calcaterra SL, Keniston A, Steeger CM, Kruse GR

item.title: Behavioral economic analysis of the reinforcing effects of fentanyl, cocaine, and mixtures of fentanyl and cocaine in rats
item.description:
Background: The co-use of opioids, primarily fentanyl, and stimulants has resulted in substantial increases in fatal multi-drug overdoses, yet few studies have systematically investigated the reinforcing effects of fentanyl + stimulant mixtures. Behavioral economic demand curve analyses can quantify the relative value of drug reinforcers across different classes (e.g., opioids and stimulants), making it a valuable method to determine factors that promote polysubstance use.

Methods: The current study used a multiple-component drug self-administration procedure to assess economic demand for fentanyl (0.00032-0.01mg/kg/inf), cocaine (0.032-1.0mg/kg/inf), and mixtures of fentanyl:cocaine at fixed-ratios of 10:1, 3:1, 1:1, 1:3, 1:10 (relative to the dose ranges used for each drug alone) in male and female Sprague-Dawley rats. Available unit doses of drug increased within-session across four components and response requirement (fixed-ratio; FR) increased across sessions. Demand curves for fentanyl, cocaine, and fentanyl:cocaine mixtures were generated, and elasticity coefficients (ɑ) estimated from demand curve analyses were used to assess the reinforcing value of the drugs alone and mixtures.

Results: Demand for cocaine was more inelastic than demand for fentanyl (i.e., cocaine was a more valuable reinforcer); demand elasticity for the mixtures became more elastic as the proportion of fentanyl to cocaine increased, and more inelastic as the proportion of cocaine to fentanyl increased.

Conclusions: These findings suggest that interactions between the reinforcing effects of fentanyl and cocaine are additive in nature, however, it is unclear whether similar interactions would be observed under clinically relevant states, such as physical dependence on opioids or opioid withdrawal.

Vazquez JM, Risca HI, Collins GT

item.title: Sex differences in the associations between symptom severity, social cognition, and connectivity between default mode sub-networks in alcohol use disorder
item.description:
Background: The default mode network (DMN) fractionates into well-established sub-networks that play pivotal roles in social cognition. Prefrontal nodes of DMN sub-networks are vulnerable to alcohol neurotoxicity, which may impair social function in individuals with alcohol use disorder (AUD). The current study examines interacting effects of AUD and sex on the relationship between social cognition and connectivity between DMN sub-networks.

Methods: Matched groups of males and females without (matched control: MC) and with (AUD) a lifetime diagnosis of AUD (N = 156; n = 39/group) were selected from the Human Connectome Project. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (~58min/participant) were used to compute functional connectivity between four DMN sub-networks: anterior dorsomedial (aDMN), ventromedial (vmDMN), medial temporal lobe (mtlDMN), and posterior (pDMN). Interacting effects of sex, AUD diagnosis/symptoms, and composite social cognition scores on between-network connectivity were assessed via non-parametric permutation testing.

Results: Connectivity between aDMN-mtlDMN (AUD<MC, pcor=.016) and vmDMN-pDMN (AUD>MC, pcor=.030) differed between AUD and MC. Social cognition was associated with aDMN-vmDMN connectivity (pcor=.003), with the relationship being moderated by sex, AUD-status and severity; males and females with mild AUD showed associations between aDMN-vmDMN connectivity and social cognition that were opposite to their matched counterparts. In individuals with greater symptom severity, associations between connectivity and social cognition were absent.

Conclusion: This study provides evidence for possible network connectivity-based mechanisms underpinning social cognition alterations in males and females with AUD. Findings show significant sex differences in these potential vulnerabilities, emerging at mild-to-moderate symptom severity, suggesting sex-specific treatment considerations are warranted.

Cohen-Gilbert JE, Waters A, Chernyak S, Janes AC, Killgore WDS, Greenfield SF

item.title: Declines in stimulant-involved overdose mortality occurred only with fentanyl co-involvement, United States, 2023-2024
item.description:
Background: Between 2023 and 2024, overdose mortality in the United States declined substantially. It is unclear whether declines in stimulant-involved overdose mortality reflect changes in stimulant-related mortality independent of fentanyl co-involvement.

Methods: We analyzed U.S. overdose mortality data from CDC WONDER for 2023 and 2024, stratifying stimulant-, cocaine-, psychostimulant-, and non-fentanyl opioid-involved deaths by fentanyl co-involvement (assigned ICD-10 multiple-cause code T40.4). Mortality rate ratios comparing 2024 with 2023 were calculated.

Results: The decline in stimulant-involved overdose mortality was observed only among deaths with fentanyl co-involvement. Similar patterns were observed for both cocaine- and psychostimulant-involved mortality. In contrast, non-fentanyl opioid-involved mortality declined both with and without fentanyl co-involvement, but the overall decline was predominantly associated with deaths with fentanyl co-involvement.

Conclusions: The recent decline in stimulant-involved overdose mortality was confined to deaths with fentanyl co-involvement. Non-fentanyl opioid-involved mortality declined in both strata, but the overall decline was predominantly associated with deaths with fentanyl co-involvement. These findings underscore the importance of stratifying category-specific overdose mortality by fentanyl co-involvement.
